lead: This unit explains how IoT data moves from sensors into cloud platforms, how it is analysed, and how the path is secured. After it you can size a cloud pipeline, choose between AWS IoT and Azure IoT Hub, explain big-data analytics and privacy controls, and describe WoT middleware, SDN and resource management for IoT.
about: Cloud computing turns IoT data into shared, elastic services. Chapter 5.1 explains cloud and sensor-cloud basics, deployment models, virtual machines, containers and device identity. Chapter 5.2 then applies these ideas to AWS IoT and Azure IoT Hub. Chapter 5.3 shows how streams and big data tools turn platform messages into alerts and models. Chapter 5.4 covers the security and privacy needed for those data paths. Chapter 5.5 adds Web of Things and middleware so devices appear as web resources. Chapter 5.6 explains software defined networking for programmable IoT traffic. Chapter 5.7, taught by only a few universities, covers clustering, agents and data synchronization for resource management.

chapters.idea: Cloud computing gives IoT a shared, elastic pool of computing, storage and services, and a sensor cloud exposes many physical sensors as virtual services.
chapters.depth: Cover cloud characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service. Explain software virtualization: hypervisor, guest VM, host, image; containerization: image, container, namespace, cgroup, Docker-style packaging; VM provisioning and manageability: templates, scaling, monitoring, snapshots. Compare IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and deployment models: public, private, hybrid, community. Introduce IoT platform, cloud IoT architecture, IoT cloud services and identity/device management. Some syllabi call this 'Introduction to Cloud Computing' or 'cloud basics'. Keep definitions and one comparison table; no deep hypervisor internals.

figure.title: Sensor cloud path
figure.aria: Water-meter readings pass from sensor nodes through a gateway to a cloud broker, then to virtual sensors and a billing application.

chapters.example: An apartment water-meter cloud serves 200 meters. Each meter sends one 64-byte reading every 30 minutes. Find readings per day, raw data per day, and raw data stored for 90 days (use 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes). Answer: 200 × 48 = 9,600 readings/day; 9,600 × 64 = 614,400 bytes/day = 0.6144 MB/day; 90 days = 55,296,000 bytes = 55.296 MB.
chapters.trap: A container is not a small VM; it shares the host kernel and needs the same OS family. A sensor cloud is not just cloud storage.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 logical design and communication models; Unit 2 sensor nodes; Unit 3 MQTT basics.
chapters.leave: Hypervisor internals and VM scheduling to operating systems; sensor hardware and MQTT packet format to Units 2 and 3.

chapters.idea: An IoT cloud platform provides device identity, a message broker, rules and storage so many devices can connect securely without custom servers.
chapters.depth: Cover the common services of AWS IoT Core and Azure IoT Hub: device registry and credentials, MQTT/TLS or AMQP endpoints, device shadows/twins, rules engine, routing to storage and functions, monitoring and device management. Compare in a table: certificates vs SAS tokens, topics vs routes, shadow vs twin. Include cloud IoT architecture and IoT cloud services. Some syllabi put this under 'Introduction to IoT Platform' or 'IoT Platform'. Do not teach MQTT packet format here.

figure.title: IoT platform pipeline
figure.aria: Five hundred soil-moisture devices publish over MQTT to a cloud IoT platform, which routes messages through rules to storage and a dashboard.

chapters.example: A farm has 500 soil-moisture devices. Each device publishes one 200-byte message every 10 minutes. Find messages per day, data per day in MB (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes), and peak message rate if all 500 publish within one 60-second window. Answer: 500 × 6 × 24 = 72,000 messages/day; 72,000 × 200 = 14,400,000 bytes/day = 14.4 MB/day; peak = 500 ÷ 60 = 8.33 messages/s.
chapters.trap: Treating AWS IoT Core and Azure IoT Hub as only brokers; exams ask identity, shadow/twin and rules too. Do not mix device shadow (AWS) with device twin (Azure).
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1 cloud models; Unit 3 MQTT; Unit 1 IoT functional blocks.
chapters.leave: MQTT publish-subscribe details to Unit 3; dashboard design to Chapter 5.3.

chapters.idea: IoT analytics turns high-volume sensor streams into useful summaries, alerts and models by combining stream processing, batch storage and visualization.
chapters.depth: Cover data and analytics for IoT: volume, velocity, variety, veracity; stream vs batch; windowing, filtering, aggregation, edge pre-processing; time-series storage; big data tools such as Hadoop HDFS and MapReduce, Spark, Kafka-style ingestion, NoSQL stores. Explain visualization: dashboards, plots, alerts. Mention Industry 4.0 predictive maintenance and sensor nodes in simple terms. Some syllabi call this 'Data Analytics for IoT' and 'Big Data Analytics tools and technology'. Keep tool internals light.

figure.title: Edge and cloud analytics
figure.aria: A sensor stream splits into a one-minute window filter and a raw store; recent values feed a live dashboard while raw data trains a daily batch model.

chapters.example: A vibration sensor samples 2,000 times per second, 4 bytes per sample. Find raw data per hour. If the edge keeps only a one-minute average (one value per minute) for the dashboard, find the reduction factor in stored values per hour. Answer: 2,000 × 3,600 = 7,200,000 samples/hour; × 4 = 28,800,000 bytes/hour = 28.8 MB/hour; dashboard values = 60/hour; reduction = 7,200,000 ÷ 60 = 120,000×.
chapters.trap: Confusing sampling rate with number of bytes; raw data per hour must multiply samples by bytes. A one-minute average does not store every raw sample.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 sensor sampling; Chapter 5.2 platform routing; basic DBMS.
chapters.leave: Sensor calibration to Unit 2; detailed Hadoop and Spark programming to a big-data course.

chapters.idea: IoT security protects device identity, data in transit and at rest, and access, while privacy limits what personal data is collected and shared.
chapters.depth: Cover security goals: confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, authorization, non-repudiation. Device identity: certificates, keys, secure boot, hardware root of trust. Network security: TLS/DTLS, MQTT over TLS, network segmentation. Access control: least privilege, roles, token expiry. Privacy: data minimisation, consent, retention, anonymisation. Mention common attacks: replay, spoofing, botnet, side-channel, and controls. Some syllabi call this 'Security in IoT protocols'. Keep protocol details light.

figure.aria: A smart lock requests a certificate, receives it, completes a TLS handshake with the broker, and sends encrypted state messages.

chapters.example: A smart-lock fleet has 10,000 devices. Each device certificate is 1 KB and rotates every 90 days. Find active certificate storage in MB (1 MB = 1000 KB) and certificates issued per year (365 days). Answer: active storage = 10,000 KB = 10 MB; issued per year = 10,000 × 365 ÷ 90 = 40,555.6 ≈ 40,556 certificates.
chapters.trap: Using encryption alone as full security; authentication and access control are separate. Do not count old certificates as active storage.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.2 device identity; Unit 3 protocol security; basic cryptography.
chapters.leave: Detailed AES and RSA math to cryptography; application login design to Chapter 5.5.

chapters.idea: The Web of Things exposes devices as web resources with descriptions and standard APIs, and IoT middleware hides protocol and hardware differences from applications.
chapters.depth: Cover WoT building blocks: Thing Description, servient, protocol binding, JSON/HTTP APIs, resource model. Middleware functions: discovery, naming, protocol translation, data aggregation, caching, event filtering, security mediation. Mention constrained devices and web-enabled constrained devices. Compare WoT with direct MQTT. Some syllabi call this 'IoT Middleware', and only some cover WoT in depth.

figure.aria: A web application talks to a WoT servient, which maps Thing Descriptions to CoAP or MQTT and then to the physical device.

chapters.example: A gateway exposes 20 sensors as WoT Things. Each Thing Description is 1.2 KB. Compression reduces size by 40%. Find stored size for all descriptions after compression. Answer: 20 × 1.2 = 24 KB; after 40% reduction = 24 × 0.6 = 14.4 KB.
chapters.trap: Thinking WoT replaces MQTT or CoAP; it is an abstraction layer that uses them. A Thing Description is metadata, not sensor data.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 MQTT/CoAP and service discovery; Chapter 5.2 cloud platform APIs.
chapters.leave: HTTP verb details to web technology; MQTT topics to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Software defined networking separates the control plane from the data plane so a central controller can program IoT traffic paths and policies.
chapters.depth: Cover SDN architecture: application plane, control plane, data plane; controller; southbound API such as OpenFlow; northbound API; flow table, match-action rules. Benefits for IoT: centralized policy, traffic engineering, slicing, quick reroute; limits: controller scaling, single point of failure, latency. Mention SDN for sensor gateways and fog nodes. Some syllabi call this 'SDN for IoT' only at overview level.

figure.aria: One SDN controller sends flow rules to five IoT gateways, and the gateways forward data to a cloud application.

chapters.example: A site has 200 sensor nodes spread over 5 equal gateways. Static routing sends 40 flows to each gateway. SDN moves 30% of the flows from one congested gateway to the other four equally. Find the final flows per gateway. Answer: initial 200 ÷ 5 = 40; moved = 0.30 × 40 = 12; congested gateway = 28; each other gateway = 40 + 12 ÷ 4 = 43; total = 28 + 4 × 43 = 200.
chapters.trap: Confusing control plane with data plane; flow rules do not carry sensor payload. The SDN controller is not the cloud application.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 network layer basics; Chapter 5.2 cloud routing; Chapter 5.5 middleware.
chapters.leave: OpenFlow message formats to a networking course; IoT routing protocols to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Resource management in large IoT systems groups nodes into clusters, uses agents for local decisions, and synchronizes replicated data so gateways and cloud stay consistent.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover clustering goals: energy saving, fewer gateway messages, cluster head election, cluster size trade-off. Agents: mobile or stationary software acting for a node or user, local filtering, negotiation. Data synchronization: replication, version vectors, conflict detection, eventual consistency, sync frequency. Keep algorithms at block level; no deep distributed-systems proofs.

figure.aria: A gateway connects to three cluster heads, each standing for ten sensor nodes.

chapters.example: A field has 30 sensor nodes in 3 clusters of 10. Directly, each node sends a 64-byte reading to the gateway every 60 s. With clustering, each node sends the same 64-byte reading to its cluster head every 60 s, and each head sends one 128-byte aggregate to the gateway every 60 s. Compare gateway inbound bytes per day (1 day = 86,400 s). Answer: direct = 30 × 1,440 × 64 = 2,764,800 bytes/day = 2.7648 MB/day; clustered gateway = 3 × 1,440 × 128 = 552,960 bytes/day = 0.55296 MB/day; reduction = 5×.
chapters.trap: Counting cluster-head traffic as extra gateway traffic without checking the reduction; also treating synchronization as instant consistency.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 WSN basics; Unit 3 network layer; Chapter 5.2 cloud routing.
chapters.leave: Detailed consensus algorithms to a distributed systems course; WSN coverage to Unit 2.
